Performance, under the hood · Puzzle 2 · 3 of 6

Slow isn't always busy

A trace section on your main thread takes 120 ms, but a sample of the same moment shows almost nothing running. Both are right. Here's the line under every thread in a system trace that explains it.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 0: A photo or a diary

    Sampling asks the kernel to snapshot a thread's call stack every so many CPU events; counting the snapshots shows where time goes, cheaply, but short calls can be missed. Method tracing injects a timestamp at every method's start and end: exact counts, but the instrumentation slows the app and skews the timings. Trace sections mark only the spans you choose.

  • Puzzle 1: Reading the flames

    A call chart draws each call along a timeline, callees under their caller. A flame chart merges identical call stacks into one bar, so width means total time and left to right means nothing. A wide bar with a wide child is slow because of the child; a bar wider than all its children is slow in its own code: its self time.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 2 puzzles: 0 → 1. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

You wrapped loadUser() in a trace section (puzzle 0) and it's 120 ms long, on the main thread, during startup. You sample the same moment: the main thread's stack barely shows up, as if it did nothing. Is the code slow, or not?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

A span on a timeline says when something started and ended. It doesn't say whether the thread was working. For that, a system trace draws a coloured state line on every thread's track: its thread state, as the kernel's scheduler (the part that decides which thread runs on which CPU) records it.

  • Running: the thread is on a CPU, executing. Only this time is "your code being slow".
  • Runnable: ready to run, but every CPU is busy with other threads. It waits its turn.
  • Sleeping: nothing to do until something happens: a lock held by another thread, a Binder reply from another process, a message.
  • Uninterruptible Sleep: waiting inside the kernel, usually for disk I/O to complete.

Sampling (puzzle 0) only fires while a thread is on a CPU, so a thread that isn't Running collects almost no samples. That's why your 120 ms span barely shows: most of it the main thread was asleep.

So before you optimise a slow span, read its states. Mostly Running: make the code faster, the flame chart (puzzle 1) shows where. Mostly Sleeping: find who it's waiting for; the trace shows which thread woke it. Mostly Uninterruptible Sleep: it's reading the disk, so move that off the main thread. Mostly Runnable: other threads, maybe your own, are keeping the CPUs busy.

The analogy

A waiter is away from your table for ten minutes. Was he slow to carry plates (Running)? Queuing for the one coffee machine (Runnable)? Waiting for the kitchen to call him (Sleeping)? Down in the cellar fetching a bottle (Uninterruptible Sleep)? The ten minutes look the same from your table; only watching him tells you which.

Check yourself

In another trace, a 120 ms main-thread span is 110 ms Sleeping. What will making its code faster save?

Not quite. Only Running time is code running; Sleeping is waiting for something else.

Right. Faster code shortens only Running.

Not quite. Sleeping ends when what it waits for arrives, not when the CPU is faster.

A span is mostly Uninterruptible Sleep. What is the thread most likely doing?

Right. Uninterruptible Sleep usually means disk I/O.

Not quite. Running is its own state; in Uninterruptible Sleep the thread isn't on a CPU.

Not quite. That's Runnable: ready, but no CPU is free.

What's the difference between Runnable and Sleeping?

Right. Ready but no CPU vs not ready.

Not quite. That's the two swapped. Re-read that part ↑

Sources

  • Android Developers: Navigate a Systrace report ("Running: The thread is completing work related to a process or is responding to an interrupt. Runnable: The thread is available to run but isn't currently scheduled. Sleeping: The thread has no work to do, perhaps because the thread is blocked on a mutex lock. Uninterruptable sleep: The thread is blocked on I/O or waiting for a disk operation to complete.")
  • Perfetto: CPU scheduling events ("When Thread A suspends on the wait() it will enter the state S(sleeping) and get removed from the CPU run queue"; end_state "R Runnable … S Sleeping D Uninterruptible Sleep")

What you now know

A system trace shows each thread's state as the kernel sees it: Running on a CPU, Runnable and waiting for one, Sleeping while blocked on a lock or a reply, or in Uninterruptible Sleep waiting for disk I/O. A slow span that's mostly Running needs faster code; mostly Sleeping or Uninterruptible Sleep, it's waiting on something else; mostly Runnable, other threads have the CPUs.
